pathogen_scientific_name.quote: The primary pathogen that causes anthracnose in the Midwest is the fungus Colletotrichum truncatum

type_of_disease.quote: Anthracnose is a fungal disease affecting maturing soybean stems and pods.

affected_parts.quote: Irregular brown spots develop in a random pattern on stems and pods. Brown cankers can appear on petioles and cause defoliation. Infected leaves may develop brown veins and curl up. Infection of pods results in few or small seeds per pod. Infected seeds may have no symptoms or may develop brown or gray areas with black specks. Infected seedlings develop dark, sunken cankers on the cotyledons, epicotyl, and radicle

summary.value: Red to brown dark irregular lesions appear on stems, pods, and petioles covered with black fruiting bodies (acervuli) containing spines (setae); affected leaves show vein reddening and rolling; symptoms are often not visible until plants approach maturity.
summary.quote: Anthracnose presents with red to brown dark irregular lesions on stems, pods, and petioles... Later during infection, fruiting bodies can be observed as black dots (acervuli) containing spines (setae) on the external surface of infected tissue. Leaf symptoms include vein reddening and leaf rolling.

diagnostic_features.value: Black fruiting bodies (acervuli) containing spines (setae) visible as black dots on infected tissue surface; tiny black spines (setae) also visible with a 10X hand lens on infected areas
diagnostic_features.quote: Later during infection, fruiting bodies can be observed as black dots (acervuli) containing spines (setae) on the external surface of infected tissue.

look_alikes.quote: Although the symptoms of anthracnose can be mistaken for pod and stem blight, the symptoms are different and both diseases may be present on the same plants late in the season.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Alfalfa mosaic virus (AMV), also known as Lucerne mosaic virus or Potato calico virus, is a worldwide distributed phytopathogen

type_of_disease.quote: Species of virus

affected_parts.quote: The virus can be detected in each part of the host plant. Transmission of the virus occurs mainly by some aphids (plant lice), by seeds or by pollen to the seed.

summary.value: Symptoms vary from wilting, white flecks, malformation like dwarfing, ringspots, mottles, mosaics to necrosis depending on the virus strain, host variety, stage of growth at infection and environmental conditions.
summary.quote: Symptoms vary from wilting, white flecks, malformation like dwarfing, ringspots, mottles, mosaics to necrosis depending on the virus strain, host variety, stage of growth at infection and environmental conditions.

diagnostic_features.value: Necrosis and yellow mosaics on affected plant tissues
diagnostic_features.quote: can lead to necrosis and yellow mosaics on a large variety of plant species

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Pod and stem blight is caused by the fungus Diaporthe sojae and D. longicolla

type_of_disease.quote: Pod and stem blight is caused by the fungus Diaporthe sojae and D. longicolla

affected_parts.quote: Pycnidia are small, black spore-producing structures that are first seen on the petioles of shed leaves... the appearance of lines of pycnidia, which may cover large sections of the stem... Pycnidia can also occur in a scattered arrangement on the pods... Infected seeds may appear healthy, or they may be shriveled and cracked.

summary.value: The most obvious sign of pod and stem blight is the presence of pycnidia on infected material - small, black spore-producing structures first seen on leaf petioles that form linear rows on stems, clusters near nodes, and scattered arrangements on pods, with infected seeds appearing shriveled, cracked, or chalky.
summary.quote: The most obvious sign of pod and stem blight is the presence of pycnidia on infected material. Pycnidia are small, black spore-producing structures that are first seen on the petioles of shed leaves... Infected seeds may appear healthy, or they may be shriveled and cracked. Infected seed are often covered with white mycelium and appear chalky.

diagnostic_features.value: The appearance of lines of pycnidia covering large sections of the stem or occurring in clusters near the nodes are the most definitive diagnostic features.
diagnostic_features.quote: One of the most definitive diagnostic features of pod and stem blight is the appearance of lines of pycnidia, which may cover large sections of the stem. These may also occur in clusters near the nodes.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Bacterial pustule is caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. glycines

type_of_disease.quote: Bacterial pustule is caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. glycines

affected_parts.quote: Symptoms begin as small, light green spots (not water-soaked) with raised centers on the upper and lower surfaces of leaves... Small raised spots may also develop on pods

summary.value: Symptoms begin as small, light green spots (not water-soaked) with raised centers on the upper and lower surfaces of leaves. Light-colored pustules (blisters) often develop in the center of lesions, especially on the undersides of leaves. The lesions can grow together into large irregular brown areas.
summary.quote: Symptoms begin as small, light green spots (not water-soaked) with raised centers on the upper and lower surfaces of leaves. Light-colored pustules (blisters) often develop in the center of lesions, especially on the undersides of leaves. The lesions can grow together into large irregular brown areas.

diagnostic_features.value: Bacterial pustule can be differentiated by a lack of water soaking at the initial site of infection, less chlorosis around lesions, and by the formation of tiny tan bumps on the undersides of leaves. Unlike soybean rust, bacterial pustule pustules lack an opening in the pustules or masses of spores. If an opening is present, it is typically a linear crack across the surface of the pustule.
diagnostic_features.quote: Bacterial pustule can be differentiated by a lack of water soaking at the initial site of infection, less chlorosis around lesions, and by the formation of tiny tan bumps on the undersides of leaves... bacterial pustule does not have an opening in the pustules or masses of spores like those of soybean rust

look_alikes.quote: Early symptoms of bacterial pustule look similar to bacterial blight... The pustules can be mistaken for those of soybean rust

conflicts.note: soybeanresearchinfo.com uses the older synonym Xanthomonas campestris pv. glycines; UNL CropWatch and UMN Extension use Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. glycines, which is the more widely cited current name in extension literature. No NCBI/MycoBank validation was returned to adjudicate.
UNL CropWatch lists only foliar symptoms; UMN Extension and soybeanresearchinfo.com both mention pods as well.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Bean pod mottle is caused by bean pod mottle virus (BPMV).

type_of_disease.quote: BPMV is a member of the genus Comovirus in the family Comoviridae.

affected_parts.quote: Symptoms associated with BPMV include mild to severe chlorotic mottling or mosaic and rugosity (distortion or wrinkling) on foliage and pods, stunting, and delayed maturity. One effect of delayed maturity is green stem where the stem remains green after the soybean pods have matured. Infection by BPMV decreases pod formation and reduces seed size, weight, and number. Seed coat mottling (the discoloration of the seed due to a black or brown pigmentation bleeding from the hilum) is another symptom caused by BPMV infection.

summary.value: Symptoms first appear on younger leaves and range from mild chlorotic mottling of foliage to severe mosaic with rugosity (distortion or wrinkling) on foliage and pods, accompanied by stunting and delayed maturity. Severe infections also produce leaf distortion, puckering, and reduced pod size. Seed coat mottling with black or brown pigmentation bleeding from the hilum is also observed.
summary.quote: Symptoms first appear on the younger leaves and can range from mild chlorotic mottling of foliage to a severe mosaic ( Figure 2 ). Green stem may also occur. In severe infections, stunting, leaf distortion and puckering and reduced pod size are also common.

diagnostic_features.value: Rugosity and chlorotic mottling on leaves and pods. Green stem where the stem remains green after the soybean pods have matured. Seed coat mottling with black or brown pigmentation bleeding from the hilum.
diagnostic_features.quote: Note the rugosity and chlorotic mottling observed on the soybean leaves. One effect of delayed maturity is green stem where the stem remains green after the soybean pods have matured. Seed coat mottling (the discoloration of the seed due to a black or brown pigmentation bleeding from the hilum) is another symptom caused by BPMV infection.

look_alikes.quote: Bean pod mottle virus symptoms are commonly confused with herbicide injury and can resemble symptoms of other viruses.

conflicts.canonical_value: Foliar, Pod, Seed, Stem, Whole plant
conflicts.note: NC State Extension lists foliar, stem, and pod but does not explicitly mention seed or whole-plant symptoms. SDSU Extension additionally documents seed coat mottling and whole-plant effects (stunting, delayed maturity).

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Septoria glycines is one of the many fungal pathogens that cause necrotic spots on leaves of soybean.

type_of_disease.quote: Soybean brown spot, also known as septoria brown spot, is caused by the fungal pathogen Septoria glycines.

affected_parts.quote: Irregular brown lesions with indefinite borders may also develop on infected pods, stems and petioles.

summary.value: Angular, red to brown spots appear on leaves that vary from tiny specks to quarter-inch diameter, causing affected leaves to turn yellow and fall to the ground; defoliation proceeds from the bottom of the plant toward the top. Initial symptoms are small dark brown spots (less than 1/8 inch) that appear first on lower leaves and progress upward.
summary.quote: Angular, red to brown spots that vary in size from tiny specks to quarter-inch diameter can be seen on the upper and lower leaf surfaces. Leaves with numerous spots rapidly turn yellow and fall to the ground. Defoliation proceeds from the bottom of the plant toward the top of the plant.

diagnostic_features.value: Angular red to brown lesions of varying sizes on leaf surfaces; brown areas contain tiny raised specks called pycnidia (visible with a hand lens) where spores are produced; rapid yellowing of heavily spotted leaves; irregular brown lesions with indefinite borders may also appear on pods, stems, and petioles.
diagnostic_features.quote: The brown areas can contain tiny raised specks called pycnidia (visible with a hand lens) where spores are produced.

look_alikes.quote: Where soybean rust may occur, it can create diagnostic problems because these two diseases can cause similar small, dark spots on leaves.

conflicts.note: NC State and UMN only mention foliar symptoms; OSU Ohioline also documents stem and pod involvement.
NC State lists only bacterial blight as a look-alike; UMN also lists soybean rust.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Bacterial blight is caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. glycinea

type_of_disease.quote: Bacterial blight is caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. glycinea, which can also infect snap bean and lima bean.

affected_parts.quote: Bacterial blight can occur on all above ground plant parts, but is most evident on leaves in the mid to upper canopy. Infection can also occur on stems, petioles, pods, and seeds in infected pods.

summary.value: Early season infection shows brown spots on cotyledons. Later symptoms include angular lesions on leaves progressing from yellow-brown to dark reddish-brown centers with yellowish-green halos around water-soaked tissue, spots merging into large dead patches; infected tissue may fall out giving leaves a ragged appearance.
summary.quote: Brown spots on the margins of the cotyledons characterize plants infected early in the growing season... Symptoms in later growth stages include angular lesions, which begin as small yellow to brown spots on the leaves. The centers of the spots will turn a dark reddish-brown and dry out. A yellowish-green "halo" will appear around the edge of water soaked tissue that surrounds the lesions. Eventually the lesions will fall out of the leaf and the foliage will appear ragged.

diagnostic_features.value: Angular lesions with dark reddish-brown centers and a distinctive yellowish-green halo around water-soaked tissue; lack of fungal structures in lesions
diagnostic_features.quote: A yellowish-green "halo" will appear around the edge of water soaked tissue that surrounds the lesions

look_alikes.quote: Bacterial blight can be mistaken for Septoria brown spot.

conflicts.note: UNL CropWatch uses Pseudomonas savastanoi; UMN Extension and NC State use Pseudomonas syringae pv. glycinea, which is more widely accepted in current literature.
NC State lists vascular tissue involvement rather than stems and pods explicitly.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Soybean mosaic is caused by the single-stranded positive-sense RNA soybean mosaic virus (SMV).

type_of_disease.quote: Soybean mosaic is caused by the single-stranded positive-sense RNA soybean mosaic virus (SMV).

affected_parts.quote: Symptoms of plants infected with soybean mosaic virus can range from no apparent symptoms to severely mottled and deformed leaves... Soybean mosaic virus can cause plant stunting, reduced seed size, and reduced pod number per plant. The disease is one of several factors associated with discoloration of seeds, causing a dark discoloration at the hilum.

summary.value: Symptoms range from no apparent symptoms to severely mottled and deformed leaves with light and dark green patches. Infected leaf blades become puckered along veins and curled downward. The disease causes plant stunting, reduced seed size, and reduced pod number. Seeds may also develop mottling symptoms.
summary.quote: Symptoms of plants infected with soybean mosaic virus can range from no apparent symptoms to severely mottled and deformed leaves. Mottling appears as light and dark green patches on individual leaves. Symptoms are most obvious on young, rapidly growing leaves. Infected leaf blades can become puckered along the veins and curled downward. Soybean mosaic virus can cause plant stunting, reduced seed size, and reduced pod number per plant.

diagnostic_features.value: Mottled leaves with contrasting light and dark green patches most obvious on young, rapidly growing leaves, with leaf blades puckered along veins and curled downward; combined with chlorosis between dark green areas.
diagnostic_features.quote: Mottling appears as light and dark green patches on individual leaves. Symptoms are most obvious on young, rapidly growing leaves. Infected leaf blades can become puckered along the veins and curled downward.

look_alikes.quote: Symptoms are often confused with growth regulator herbicide damage where the leaves will be elongated and which usually occurs in a pattern such as along a field edge.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: plants infected with bean pod mottle virus may be predisposed to seed infection by Phomopsis fungi that also reduce seed quality

type_of_disease.quote: Phomopsis fungi

affected_parts.quote: seed infection by Phomopsis fungi

summary.value: Phomopsis fungi reduce seed quality.
summary.quote: Phomopsis fungi that also reduce seed quality

affected_parts.quote: Brown stem rot (BSR) has very similar leaf symptoms to SDS... Plants infected by BSR have a tan to brown pith at or near the crown, and often at the leaf nodes.

summary.value: Similar leaf symptoms to SDS, but with tan to brown pith at or near the crown and at leaf nodes
summary.quote: Brown stem rot (BSR) has very similar leaf symptoms to SDS. Plants infected by BSR have a tan to brown pith at or near the crown, and often at the leaf nodes.

diagnostic_features.value: Tan to brown pith at crown and leaf nodes distinguishes it from SDS, which has white pith
diagnostic_features.quote: Plants infected by BSR have a tan to brown pith at or near the crown, and often at the leaf nodes. SDS-infected soybeans retain a white pith.

look_alikes.quote: Brown stem rot (BSR) has very similar leaf symptoms to SDS.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: The causal agent of Soybean Sudden Death Syndrome (SDS) is the soil borne fungus Fusarium virguliforme

type_of_disease.quote: the soil borne fungus Fusarium virguliforme

affected_parts.quote: Symptoms begin in the roots and include necrosis and dieback... The vascular tissue of the taproot becomes brown and discolored. This discoloration can extend upward to the lower stem... the leaves initially develop intravenous chlorotic spots that soon become necrotic

summary.value: Root symptoms include necrosis and dieback with brown vascular discoloration extending to the lower stem. Foliar symptoms develop with interveinal chlorotic spots that become necrotic, with leaflets eventually detaching from petioles while the central vein remains green.
summary.quote: Symptoms begin in the roots and include necrosis and dieback, similar to other root diseases... The vascular tissue of the taproot becomes brown and discolored... the leaves initially develop intravenous chlorotic spots that soon become necrotic... only the central vein remains green and leaflets begin to detach from the petioles.

diagnostic_features.value: White pith at the crown distinguishes SDS from Brown Stem Rot, which has tan to brown pith. Blue-green masses of macroconidia may be visible on roots close to the soil line, and interveinal chlorosis with central vein remaining green on leaves.
diagnostic_features.quote: SDS-infected soybeans retain a white pith. Plants infected by BSR have a tan to brown pith at or near the crown

look_alikes.quote: SDS can be easily confused with other root rot diseases, including Fusarium wilt, Phytophthora root rot, and white mold. The foliar symptoms caused by SDS can sometimes be mistaken for a virus, like soybean vein necrosis virus

conflicts.alternative_value: Fusarium virgulifome (typo; previously named Fusarium solani f.sp. glycines)
conflicts.note: UMN Extension contains a typographical error 'virgulifome'; NC State and OSU both cite the correct spelling 'virguliforme'. The synonym Fusarium solani f. sp. glycines is noted by UMN.

diagnostic_features.value: Soybean rust pustules have an opening and masses of spores, unlike bacterial pustule.
diagnostic_features.quote: bacterial pustule does not have an opening in the pustules or masses of spores like those of soybean rust

look_alikes.quote: The pustules can be mistaken for those of soybean rust

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Cercospora leaf blight is caused by the fungus Cercospora kikuchii

type_of_disease.quote: Cercospora leaf blight is caused by the fungus Cercospora kikuchii

affected_parts.quote: Red-brown spots may develop on both leaf surfaces. The spots may coalesce to form large necrotic areas on leaves. Reddish-purple lesions may also occur on petioles, stems, and pods. Infected seeds have pink to purple discoloration on the seed coats.

summary.value: The first symptom of Cercospora leaf blight is the development of light purple spots and areas on the top surface of leaves exposed to light. The discolored areas expand and deepen in color to a reddish-purple or bronze. The infected leaves appear leathery and 'sunburned'. Infected seeds have pink to purple discoloration on the seed coats.
summary.quote: The first symptom of Cercospora leaf blight is the development of light purple spots and areas on the top surface of leaves exposed to light. The discolored areas expand and deepen in color to a reddish-purple or bronze. The infected leaves appear leathery and 'sunburned'. Infected seeds have pink to purple discoloration on the seed coats.

diagnostic_features.value: Light purple spots on upper leaf surfaces that expand and coalesce into large necrotic areas; leaves appear leathery and sunburned; reddish-purple lesions on petioles, stems, and pods; pink to purple discoloration on seed coats. Seed discoloration may range from small spots to coverage of the entire seed surface.
diagnostic_features.quote: The first symptom of Cercospora leaf blight is the development of light purple spots and areas on the top surface of leaves exposed to light. The discolored areas expand and deepen in color to a reddish-purple or bronze. The infected leaves appear leathery and 'sunburned'. Red-brown spots may develop on both leaf surfaces. The spots may coalesce to form large necrotic areas on leaves. Reddish-purple lesions may also occur on petioles, stems, and pods. Infected seeds have pink to purple discoloration on the seed coats.

conflicts.canonical_value: Cercospora Leaf Blight and Purple Seed Stain
conflicts.alternative_value: purple seed stain (treated as separate disease)
conflicts.note: CABI and UDel treat purple seed stain as a distinct named disease; UMN and UDel also list both under one combined heading. Merged here as one disease entity caused by the same pathogen.
UDel foliar-symptom entry lists only Foliar; UMN lists Foliar, Stem, Pod, Seed; CABI lists Seed, Foliar, Pod. Canonical value is the superset from the highest-ranked source (UMN).

pathogen_scientific_name.value: Diaporthe phaseolorum var. caulivora and Diaporthe phaseolorum var. meridionalis
pathogen_scientific_name.quote: caused by the fungal pathogens Diaporthe phaseolorum var. caulivora and Diaporthe phaseolorum var. meridionalis

type_of_disease.quote: caused by the fungal pathogens Diaporthe phaseolorum var. caulivora and Diaporthe phaseolorum var. meridionalis

affected_parts.quote: Early symptoms are reddish-brown lesions that appear at the base of branches or leaf petioles... Reddish-brown discoloration may also occur inside the stem, and pods can abort. Leaves may develop necrosis and chlorosis between the veins

summary.value: Initial reddish-brown lesions appear at the base of branches or leaf petioles and on stems during early reproductive stages, progressing to dark brown or black sunken cankers that girdle and kill the stem. Foliage exhibits interveinal chlorosis that becomes necrotic; leaves may remain attached after death.
summary.quote: initial symptoms of infection are reddish-brown lesions that can be observed on the stem during late vegetative growth stages and into reproductive growth stages. As the disease progresses, the lesions expand turning dark brown or black in color and can extend over several nodes. The lesions become sunken cankers that girdle the stem, killing the plant. Upon infection, interveinal chlorosis may be a foliar symptom that becomes necrotic as the disease progresses.

diagnostic_features.value: Sunken cankers enlarge longitudinally, turn dark brown to black, and girdle the stem; green stem tissue is usually present both above and below individual stem cankers; tiny black dots (perithecia or stroma/fruiting bodies) appear on dead stem tissue; reddish-brown discoloration may occur inside the stem; cankers typically form higher on the plant than Phytophthora.
diagnostic_features.quote: A diagnostic symptom of stem canker is that green stem tissue will usually be present both above and below individual stem cankers... cankers will enlarge, longitudinally, turn dark brown to black in color, become slightly sunken... stem canker usually forms higher on the plant than does Phytophthora

look_alikes.quote: It can be confused with Phytophtora rot... Lesions often develop at and remain darker at nodes, but may extend to the soil line and create a situation easily confused with Phytophthora rot.

conflicts.canonical_value: Diaporthe phaseolorum var. caulivora and Diaporthe phaseolorum var. meridionalis
conflicts.note: Nebraska CropWatch notes only northern stem canker (D. phaseolorum var. caulivora) has been observed in Nebraska; NC State and UMN Extension both recognize two causal pathogens (northern and southern variants).

conflicts.canonical_value: Stem, Leaves, Vascular tissue, Pod, Seed
conflicts.alternative_value: Stem, Leaves, Vascular tissue (no seed mention)
conflicts.note: Nebraska CropWatch does not mention seed infection; NC State Extension explicitly notes seed can also be infected.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Charcoal rot is caused by the soilborne fungus Macrophomina phaseolina

type_of_disease.quote: caused by the soilborne fungus Macrophomina phaseolina

affected_parts.quote: soilborne root and stem disease of soybean... leaflets on infected plants may be small and ultimately wilt and turn brown. The taproot and lower stem may become streaked with light gray... Reddish-brown discoloration can also develop in the pith and vascular tissues of the root and stem

summary.value: Infected plants become wilted and stunted; fungal structures called microsclerotia fill root and stem tissues, clogging vascular tissue and causing wilting, yellowing, and stunting. Characteristic charcoal-sprinkled appearance develops on roots and stems.
summary.quote: Infected plants may die prematurely and are often wilted and stunted. Brown lesions may form on the hypocotyl of emerging seedlings... Small black specks may form beneath the epidermis and inside the lower stem and taproot to give them a charcoal-sprinkled appearance

diagnostic_features.value: Small, dark, round fungal structures called microsclerotia visible in split lower stems or when outer bark is removed; characteristic charcoal-sprinkled appearance from small black specks beneath the epidermis and inside lower stem and taproot; reddish-brown discoloration in pith and vascular tissues of root and stem; light gray streaking on taproot and lower stem.
diagnostic_features.quote: remove symptomatic plants from the soil profile and either split the lower stems or gently remove the outer bark of the plant to look for microsclerotia

look_alikes.quote: Symptoms are easy to confuse with several other diseases and disorders, including soybean cyst nematode injury, early senescence and drought stress. A description of how to distinguish charcoal rot from the zone lines associated with Diaporthe diseases, can be found in the publication.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Fusarium wilt is a disease complex caused by several soil-borne fungi, commonly Fusarium oxysporum.

type_of_disease.quote: Fusarium oxysporum is an ascomycete fungus found commonly in the soil.

affected_parts.quote: Foliar symptoms include interveinal chlorosis, premature defoliation and wilting. The roots often decay with brown to black epidermal tissues and reddish to brown vascular discoloration extending into the stem.

summary.value: Root rot appears as reddish-brown to dark brown discolored roots and poor nodulation. Foliar symptoms of Fusarium wilt include scorching of the upper leaves, while middle and lower canopy leaves can turn chlorotic and later wither and drop from the plant. Infected plants have brown vascular tissue in the roots and stems and show wilting of the stem tips.
summary.quote: Root rot appears as reddish-brown to dark brown discolored roots and poor nodulation. Foliar symptoms of Fusarium wilt include scorching of the upper leaves, while middle and lower canopy leaves can turn chlorotic and later wither and drop from the plant.

diagnostic_features.value: Brown vascular tissue in roots and stems, wilting of stem tips, and the absence of external decay or stem lesions above the soil line. In plant stems, the fungus may produce a purple to pink vascular discoloration.
diagnostic_features.quote: Infected plants have brown vascular tissue in the roots and stems and show wilting of the stem tips. External decay or stem lesions are not seen above the soil line.

look_alikes.quote: this disease is easily confused with Verticillium wilt

conflicts.note: UMN Extension specifies a forma specialis (f. sp. lycopersici) associated with tomato; the NC State soybean source lists Fusarium oxysporum broadly. The UMN page may refer to the tomato-specific form and may not be specific to soybean.
UMN Extension includes 'Whole plant' as an affected part and does not specifically list Root separately.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Green stem syndrome refers to plants that maintain green stems and sometimes leaves well past the time when they are normally brown and mature.

affected_parts.quote: Stems of plants remain green after the pods and seeds have ripened and are brown and ready for harvest. Occasionally the stems and leaves remain green after the pods have matured

summary.value: Plants maintain green stems and sometimes leaves well past the time when they are normally brown and mature, while pods and seeds have ripened.
summary.quote: Green stem syndrome refers to plants that maintain green stems and sometimes leaves well past the time when they are normally brown and mature. The plant stems remain moist while the pods and seeds have ripened.

diagnostic_features.value: Stems remain green after pods and seeds have ripened and are brown and ready for harvest, with plant stems remaining moist.
diagnostic_features.quote: Stems of plants remain green after the pods and seeds have ripened and are brown and ready for harvest. The plant stems remain moist while the pods and seeds have ripened.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: The species most frequently associated with root rot on soybean are F. solani and F. oxysporum.

type_of_disease.quote: fungal root rot

affected_parts.quote: The lower taproot and lateral roots of infected soybean plants may appear brown to black in color and show cortical decay or vascular discoloration. If root rot becomes severe, infected soybeans may develop foliar symptoms including stunting, marginal or whole leaf chlorosis (yellowing), wilting, and defoliation.

summary.value: Lower taproot and lateral roots appear brown to black with cortical decay or vascular discoloration. If severe, infected plants develop foliar symptoms including stunting, leaf yellowing, wilting, and defoliation.
summary.quote: The lower taproot and lateral roots of infected soybean plants may appear brown to black in color and show cortical decay or vascular discoloration... If root rot becomes severe, infected soybeans may develop foliar symptoms including stunting, marginal or whole leaf chlorosis (yellowing), wilting, and defoliation.

diagnostic_features.value: Brown to black discoloration of lower taproot and lateral roots with cortical decay and vascular discoloration; lateral roots die and decompose with secondary roots developing above them on the upper taproot.
diagnostic_features.quote: The lower taproot and lateral roots of infected soybean plants may appear brown to black in color and show cortical decay or vascular discoloration. Lateral roots may also die and decompose, and secondary roots may develop above them on the upper taproot.

look_alikes.quote: Fusarium species are often isolated from soybean roots that are also infected by other pathogens (e.g. Pythium, Phytophthora, and Rhizoctonia).

conflicts.canonical_value: Fusarium Root Rot (distinct from Fusarium Wilt)
conflicts.alternative_value: Fusarium Root Rot and Wilt treated as a single disease complex
conflicts.note: Crop Protection Network treats Fusarium Root Rot and Wilt as a single combined disease entry, whereas NC State and UMN Extension treat them separately. The records have been retained as separate canonical entries to preserve all disease information.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: The pathogen that causes Phytophthora damping-off, root, and stem rot of soybean is Phytophthora sojae.

type_of_disease.quote: This is a water mold and produces oospores in infected plants.

affected_parts.quote: Phytophthora can attack soybean plants at any stage of development. Symptoms in young plants include rapid yellowing and wilting accompanied by a soft rot and collapse of the root... Foliar symptoms on older plants occur as general yellowing of the lower leaves... Perhaps the best diagnostic symptom of the disease on susceptible varieties is a lower stem discoloration that may extend several nodes up the stem.

summary.value: Young plants show rapid yellowing, wilting, soft rot, and root collapse; mature plants exhibit general yellowing of lower leaves progressing upward, wilting, and severe root discoloration with lower stem lesions.
summary.quote: Symptoms in young plants include rapid yellowing and wilting accompanied by a soft rot and collapse of the root. More mature plants generally show reduced vigor and may be gradually killed as the growing season progresses. Foliar symptoms on older plants occur as general yellowing of the lower leaves that progresses upward on the plant, followed by wilting and death.

diagnostic_features.value: Lower stem discoloration extending several nodes up the stem; severely discolored lateral and branch roots; tap roots with brown surface discoloration and tan to brown inner tissue discoloration when split.
diagnostic_features.quote: Perhaps the best diagnostic symptom of the disease on susceptible varieties is a lower stem discoloration that may extend several nodes up the stem. The root system is usually severely affected such that lateral and branch roots are almost completely discolored. Tap roots show a brown discoloration on the surface and, if split, the inner tissues show a tan to brown discoloration.

type_of_disease.quote: Pythiums are a group of fungal-like organisms (Oomycetes)

affected_parts.quote: Symptoms of pre-emergence damping-off include seeds failing to germinate and/or the total disintegration of the seed while in the soil. Post-emergence damping-off is visible first as lesions and discoloration on the roots.
